a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not

claims.claim: Bumetanide, a sulfamoyl anthranilic acid loop diuretic structurally related to the query, has an absolute oral bioavailability of 95% in cirrhosis patients after oral versus IV dosing (n=8), with L2 context reporting 95-100%; this is the most condition- and class-matched direct F evidence.
Other cirrhosis-condition contexts show high oral bioavailability (metoclopramide 79-82%, tolfenamic acid about 100%), supporting a pattern of preserved or increased F in cirrhosis.

Azosemide, the closest structural analog (sulfamoyl anthranilic acid with tetrazole/thiophene bioisosteres), has an L1 absolute oral bioavailability of 20.4% in fasted healthy humans, meeting the F>=20% threshold; the L2 10% urinary-recovery estimate is indirect and does not overturn the L1 value.

L6 hepatic-clearance records show low rat hepatic microsomal intrinsic clearance for azosemide (C69/C70) and no CYP2E1-mediated bumetanide metabolism (C77), providing limited mechanistic support for low hepatic first-pass in this structural class; no furosemide-specific hepatic clearance record is present, and species/assay differences limit transfer.

evidence_gaps: No direct oral bioavailability measurement for furosemide itself is supplied.
No furosemide-specific hepatic clearance or metabolic-stability record is supplied; L6 records are for azosemide, bumetanide, bupropion, diclofenac, GV150526, and an unrelated compound.
Azosemide was studied in fasted healthy subjects, not cirrhosis, and has conflicting estimates (20.4% L1 absolute vs 10% L2 urinary recovery).
Cirrhosis effects on furosemide-specific transporters and first-pass metabolism are not directly measured.
The physicochemical low-permeability prior is not supported by any furosemide-specific absorption or permeability record in the supplied evidence.
C75 lacks a control value and uses artificial 3-methylcholanthrene induction, so it cannot quantify normal hepatic first-pass loss.
content.decision_summary: L6 hepatic-clearance records do not provide furosemide-specific evidence; the relevant analog records (azosemide low rat microsomal CLint, bumetanide no CYP2E1 metabolism) are mechanistically supportive of limited hepatic first-pass but have low transferability. The prediction remains high, supported by condition-matched high-F analogs (bumetanide 95% in cirrhosis; metoclopramide 79-82%; tolfenamic acid about 100%) and the closest structural analog azosemide at 20.4% L1 absolute F. The indirect azosemide urinary-recovery estimate of 10% and the physicochemical low-permeability prior are insufficient to support F<20%.
